lesson_title: Scales, Directions and Slope: One Page, the Whole Garden Route
hook_text: Which trail up the mountain is steeper: 1 to 3 or 1 to 10? Most of the class gets it backwards.
clip_script: The road atlas says 1 to one and a half million. Don't panic — do one clever move: one and a half million centimetres is fifteen kilometres, so every centimetre on this page is 15 k's. Ruler on the N2: 33 centimetres. Times fifteen — 495 kilometres. The road signs say 489. The ruler told the truth to within a small town. Now leave the tar for the Outeniquas, where the map turns to brown spaghetti. Every brown line joins ground at the SAME height, ten metres between lines. Cross twelve lines? You climbed 120 metres — guaranteed. Where the lines CROWD, the mountain rears up. Now the number: gradient is climb over distance. Trail one: 120 metres up over 1 200 along — 1 to 10. Trail two: same 120 up, over just 360 — 1 to 3. So which is steeper? Say it as a sentence: one metre up every THREE steps... or one metre up every TEN. The 1 to 3 trail is the killer — smaller second number, steeper climb. Picture two ladders: 1 to 3 stands nearly upright; 1 to 10 leans back lazily. One flat page just told you how far, which way, how steep — before a single boot touched the mountain.
visual_style: A road atlas unfolding on a lounge floor, a ruler sweeping the N2 with kilometres counting up; then the map morphing into brown contour spaghetti that rises into a 3D mountain, two ladders leaning against a wall at different angles.
mood: Holiday-road breezy turning summit-serious, the confidence of a navigator.
pacing: Quick win on the 495 km calculation, slow reveal as the contours rise, punchline landing on the two ladders.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read distance, direction and steepness off any map — before your legs find out the hard way.
